title: Valle d'Aosta — Alpine Wines
quiz.0.question: How many DOCs does Valle d'Aosta have?

quiz.1.question: Valle d'Aosta's vineyards lie in the rain shadow of which mountain?
quiz.1.explanation: The vineyards lie in the rain shadow of Monte Bianco (Mont Blanc), so they are relatively dry and sunny.

slides.0.title: 🏔️ Valle d'Aosta
slides.0.subtitle: Mountain Wines Beneath Monte Bianco
slides.1.title: 📍 Regional Overview
slides.1.content:
Valle d'Aosta is Italy's smallest and least populated region, and the one producing the least wine. In the far north-west of Italy, it borders Switzerland to the north, France to the west and Piemonte to the south and east, ringed by the highest peaks of the Alps. The whole region has a single DOC: Valle d'Aosta / Vallée d'Aoste, with several sub-zones and varietal wines.

📍
Location
An Alpine valley in Italy's north-western corner, bordering Switzerland to the north, France to the west and Piemonte to the south and east; capital Aosta
🗣️
Autonomous Region
A region with special autonomous status where Italian and French are both official languages; bilingual labels and place names are common
🍷
Appellations
Only 1 DOC (Valle d'Aosta / Vallée d'Aoste) and no DOCG; 7 sub-zones plus a number of varietal wines
🏔️
Style
Mountain terroir gives fresh, high-acid wines with light to medium body; production is small and mostly consumed by locals and visitors
slides.2.title: 🏛️ History: A Valley Shaped by France
slides.2.content:
Guarding the Alpine passes to France and Switzerland — Valle d'Aosta's history and culture have long been tied to the French-speaking world

Antiquity
The Salassi and the Romans: the valley was first home to the Celtic Salassi tribe; the Romans conquered it in 25 BC and founded Augusta Praetoria (today's Aosta) to control the passes to Gaul
From the Middle Ages
The House of Savoy: the valley was long ruled by the House of Savoy, sharing a political and cultural sphere with the French-speaking lands across the Alps, which is why French became the local language of administration and daily life
Late 19th Century
Disease and decline: oidium, downy mildew and phylloxera devastated the vineyards and, together with emigration, greatly reduced the area under vine
1948
Special autonomy: the Italian Republic granted Valle d'Aosta the status of an autonomous region with special statute, with French and Italian as official languages
1971 → 1985
Appellations: early DOCs such as Donnas were created in the 1970s; in 1985 they were merged into the region-wide Valle d'Aosta / Vallée d'Aoste DOC, with the former appellations becoming sub-zones. Co-operatives and the regional agricultural school played a key role in raising quality

slides.4.title: 🌍 Topography and Climate: the Alps, Monte Bianco and the Dora Baltea
slides.4.content:
A glacial valley enclosed by mountains — the Alps, the northerly position and Monte Bianco shape Valle d'Aosta's climate

🏔️

Topography

The Alps: the whole region is mountainous, surrounded by peaks such as Monte Bianco (Mont Blanc), Monte Rosa, Cervino (the Matterhorn) and Gran Paradiso

The Dora Baltea: rising near Monte Bianco, it flows east past Aosta, then turns south-east into Piemonte and eventually joins the Po; the vineyards follow this main valley

Geology: a U-shaped valley carved by glaciers, with shallow, well-drained soils of moraine, sand and rock debris

🌤️

Climate

Continental Alpine climate: long cold winters, short warm summers and wide day-night temperature swings that preserve acidity and aroma

Rain shadow: the vineyards lie in the rain shadow of Monte Bianco, with little rain and plenty of sunshine, making this a relatively dry Alpine valley

Sunny slopes: most vineyards lie on the south-facing slopes (adret) on the north side of the valley to capture the most sun

Wind: valley breezes keep the vines ventilated and reduce disease pressure
slides.5.title: ⛰️ Elevation and Heroic Viticulture
slides.5.content:
Elevation changes everything here: training systems, rootstocks and the choice of grape varieties

🧱 Terraces and Stone Walls

Terraces built with dry-stone walls on steep slopes are worked almost entirely by hand, earning the name "heroic" viticulture. The walls absorb heat by day and release it at night, helping the grapes ripen.

🌿 Traditional Training: Pergola

Valle d'Aosta and Liguria are the northern Italian regions where the traditional pergola survives. In the Lower Valley (around Donnas) the pergolas rest on stone pillars; in Morgex in the Upper Valley low pergolas keep the grapes close to the warm ground and bear the weight of snow.

🦠 Ungrafted Old Vines

In the Upper Valley's Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle, the cold climate and sandy soils at very high elevation make life hard for phylloxera, so ungrafted Prié Blanc vines can still be found; vineyards reach about 1,200 m, among the highest in Europe.

📈 Elevation and Varieties

The higher the site, the better suited it is to early-ripening, cold-hardy whites (such as Prié Blanc); the warmer Central Valley is dominated by native reds such as Petit Rouge; only in the lower, warmer Lower Valley near Piemonte can late-ripening Nebbiolo ripen.
slides.6.title: 🍇 Native and Traditional Varieties
slides.6.content:
🔴 Native Red Grapes

Petit Rouge: the most widely planted variety and the mainstay of Central Valley sub-zones such as Torrette and Enfer d'Arvier; medium-deep colour, red fruit and spice, low to medium tannins

Fumin: deep colour, high acidity and tannin, with red fruit, herbs and spice, medium to full body

Cornalin: deep colour and fruity, the same variety as Humagne Rouge in Switzerland's Valais

Vien de Nus, Mayolet: other native reds; Vien de Nus leads the reds of the Nus sub-zone

⚪ Native White Grape

Prié Blanc: Valle d'Aosta's most important native white, grown in the high vineyards of the Upper Valley; very pale, light-bodied, high-acid whites with white flowers, green apple, citrus, mountain hay and flint; also made as sparkling wine

🍇 Traditional Varieties (Not Native but Long Established)

Nebbiolo (locally Picotendro): grown in Donnas and Arnad-Montjovet in the Lower Valley

Moscato Bianco: the signature white of Chambave, made dry and as sweet flétri

Malvoisie (Pinot Grigio): the white of Nus, also made as flétri

Petite Arvine: from Switzerland's Valais, excellent here

International varieties: Chardonnay, Pinot Nero, Müller-Thurgau, Gamay and others
slides.7.title: 🗺️ Upper, Central and Lower Valley and the Seven Sub-zones
slides.7.content:
Upper Valley — at the Foot of Monte Bianco

Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle: the villages of Morgex and La Salle, the highest and coldest sub-zone; only Prié Blanc, for still and sparkling whites, often from ungrafted vines

Central Valley — Around Aosta, Home of the Native Reds

Enfer d'Arvier: a small sub-zone at Arvier whose name means "hell", for its especially hot, rock-walled amphitheatre; reds based on Petit Rouge
Torrette: west of Aosta around Aymavilles, the largest sub-zone; reds based on Petit Rouge, including a Supérieur level
Nus: east of Aosta; reds based on the native Vien de Nus and whites from Malvoisie (Pinot Grigio), including sweet flétri
Chambave: the eastern end of the Central Valley; famous for dry and sweet flétri Moscato, plus a Petit Rouge-based red

Lower Valley — Gateway to Piemonte

Arnad-Montjovet: where the Dora Baltea turns south-east; reds based on Nebbiolo (Picotendro)
Donnas: closest to the Piemonte border, next to Piemonte's Carema; Nebbiolo (Picotendro)-based, pale, with rose, red fruit, underbrush and tar, high acidity and medium to high tannins
slides.8.title: 🏷️ Labels and Sweet Wines
slides.8.content:
Reading a Valle d'Aosta Label

With only one DOC, every label starts with Valle d'Aosta (or the French Vallée d'Aoste), followed by more specific information:

Sub-zone wines: DOC name + sub-zone, e.g. Valle d'Aosta Donnas DOC, Valle d'Aosta Torrette DOC, Valle d'Aosta Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle DOC
Varietal wines: DOC name + grape, e.g. Valle d'Aosta Fumin DOC, Valle d'Aosta Petite Arvine DOC, Valle d'Aosta Chardonnay DOC

Late Harvest (Vendemmia Tardiva) vs Passito (Flétri)

🍇 Vendemmia tardiva (late harvest)

The grapes are left on the vine and picked late, overripe and with concentrated sugar, before vinification.

☀️ Flétri (passito, dried grapes)

The grapes are dried after harvest, losing water and concentrating sugar before vinification. Flétri is Valle d'Aosta's French name for passito; the best known are Chambave Moscato Flétri and Nus Malvoisie Flétri, listed by IWS among northern Italy's main passito wines.
slides.9.title: 🍷 IWS Suggested Tasting Wines
slides.9.content:
IWS suggests tasting at least one red and one white; below are the style profiles from the course materials

🔴 Valle d'Aosta Donnas DOC (Nebbiolo)

Pale, with rose, red fruit, underbrush and tar; dry, high acidity, medium to high tannins, medium to high alcohol, medium body. Arnad-Montjovet is an alternative.

🔴 Valle d'Aosta Torrette DOC (Petit Rouge)

Medium-deep, with red fruit and spice; dry, medium acidity, low to medium tannins, medium alcohol, medium body. Enfer d'Arvier is an alternative.

🔴 Valle d'Aosta Fumin DOC

Deep, with red fruit, herbs and spice; dry, high acidity, high tannins, medium to high alcohol, medium to full body. Cornalin is an alternative.

⚪ Valle d'Aosta Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle DOC (Prié Blanc)

Very pale, with white flowers, green apple, citrus, mountain hay and herbs, mineral and flint; dry, high acidity, medium alcohol, light body.

⚪ Valle d'Aosta Petite Arvine DOC

Medium straw-yellow, with white flowers, citrus (grapefruit), pear and apple, exotic fruit, mineral and saline notes; dry, high acidity, medium to high alcohol, medium to full body. Chardonnay is an alternative.

slides.10.content:
Small volumes and fragmented plots: co-operatives and small family estates are the backbone of Valle d'Aosta wine

slides.11.title: 🍽️ Food Culture
slides.11.content:
Mountain cooking built on cheese, cured meats and stews — fresh, high-acid Valle d'Aosta wines cut through the richness

⚪ Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle

Pair with: Lardo d'Arnad and Alpine cured meats
Arnad's pork fatback cured with herbs and spices meets light, high-acid Prié Blanc for a refreshing contrast.

⚪ Petite Arvine

Pair with: Fonduta (Fontina fondue)
A fondue of local Fontina cheese, matched by Petite Arvine's fuller body and saline finish.

🔴 Torrette (Petit Rouge)

Pair with: Carbonade (beef stewed in red wine)
Cured beef braised in red wine and served with polenta; Petit Rouge's red fruit, spice and soft tannins suit the stew.

🔴 Donnas (Nebbiolo)

Pair with: game and aged Fontina
High acidity and firm tannins suit braised game and aged mountain cheese.
slides.12.title: 🎓 Key Takeaways
slides.12.points.0: ✓ Valle d'Aosta is Italy's smallest region and its smallest wine producer, an autonomous region where Italian and French are both official
slides.12.points.1: ✓ The whole region has a single DOC: Valle d'Aosta / Vallée d'Aoste, with 7 sub-zones and no DOCG
slides.12.points.2: ✓ Vineyards follow the Dora Baltea valley in the rain shadow of Monte Bianco: dry, sunny, with wide day-night temperature swings
slides.12.points.3: ✓ Long ruled by the House of Savoy, the region has deep French cultural roots, and French often appears on labels
slides.12.points.4: ✓ Heroic viticulture: dry-stone terraces and traditional pergolas; high-altitude Prié Blanc in Morgex is often ungrafted
slides.12.points.5: ✓ Upper Valley: Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle (Prié Blanc)
slides.12.points.6: ✓ Central Valley: Enfer d'Arvier, Torrette (Petit Rouge), Nus (Vien de Nus, Malvoisie), Chambave (Moscato)
slides.12.points.7: ✓ Lower Valley: Arnad-Montjovet, Donnas (Nebbiolo, locally Picotendro)
slides.12.points.8: ✓ Native varieties: Petit Rouge (most planted), Fumin, Cornalin, Vien de Nus, Mayolet, Prié Blanc; Nebbiolo, Moscato, Malvoisie and Petite Arvine are traditional varieties
slides.12.points.9: ✓ Labels: Valle d'Aosta + sub-zone (e.g. Donnas) or Valle d'Aosta + grape (e.g. Fumin, Petite Arvine)
slides.12.points.10: ✓ Late harvest (vendemmia tardiva) overripens on the vine; flétri (passito) is dried after harvest
